11.0.s.en: (1) John sends two disciples to Christ

11.0.0.en: After Christ had explained to His disciples how to preach, He presented Himself as a practical example in carrying out what He had commanded them, for He began to teach what He had taught them in the synagogues spread throughout Galilee.

11.0.1.en: Take care to carry out what you teach others, so that your words may be effective.

11.1.0.en: King Herod arrested John and put him in prison. And as John felt that his end was near, he wanted to attach his disciples to Christ, so he sent two of them with a question to Him, saying: Are you the awaited Messiah or not? John was not doubting this, because he had known Him and had bowed down to Him while still in his mother's womb, and when he baptized Him, he testified that He is "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29), that is, that He is Christ the Redeemer; but he wanted to establish the faith of these two disciples in Christ, so that they would preach to the rest of their companions, John's disciples, so that all would follow Christ.

11.2.0.en: "The poor": not only the poor and the weak, but rather the poor in spirit, that is, the humble.

11.2.1.en: Christ's answer was His miracles, which these two disciples had seen, and they were varied, and included the healing of diseases however difficult, even if they signified uncleanness, like leprosy, or deprived a person of life through death, for He is able to deliver a person from them. Consequently, they conclude from this that He is the Christ. Make your good conduct an example that preaches your Christ, especially when speaking about Christ is not possible, for deeds are stronger than words, and words without deeds are not enough.

11.3.0.en: Christ cautions the two disciples, lest they stumble or doubt Him, because some of John's disciples were jealous for him, since a better teacher than he had appeared, and many crowds were following Him (Jn 3:26); so He calls them to believe in Him, for He is the Messiah for whom John prepared the way.

11.4.0.en: "A reed": that is, a stalk of cane, and these reeds or canes were abundant at the Jordan River, where John used to baptize.

11.4.1.en: After the departure of John's two disciples, Christ spoke about him, not intending flattery, but to give true testimony to John, who prepared the way for Him, and He said: Was John a reed shaken by the wind? The reed is hollow, so it points to the person who is empty of the grace of God, and "the wind" signifies the evil thoughts of the world. So the person who has a shining appearance like the reed, and is inwardly empty of God, is affected by the winds of temptations and evil thoughts. This is not John, but he is a man full of God, preparing the way for Christ by calling people to repentance, and firm in his principles however much evil surrounds him.

11.5.0.en: Christ asks: Was John's clothing of soft garments? No... because these pampered, luxurious people sit inside the palaces in the cities.

11.5.1.en: And these garments signify the body pampered with lusts and ease, but John was ascetic, his clothing rough and his food bare, because his heart was occupied with God and His service, and he lived austerely in the wilderness. Therefore Christ declares the greatness of John and his steadfastness in the faith, and that his sending his two disciples to Him was to bind his disciples to Him, and not for his own sake.

11.6.0.en: John the Baptist was greater than all the prophets of the Old Testament, because they longed to see Christ, and did not see Him, but only prophesied about Him. But John prophesied about Him and then beheld Him, and even baptized Him, for he is the messenger who prepared the way for Christ (Mal 3:1).

11.7.0.en: John is the greatest of men, but Christ, who is younger than he by six months, is greater than he. There is another opinion, that John is the greatest of the men of the Old Testament, but the least believer in the New Testament is greater than he in respect of his enjoying the Holy Sacraments in the Church and all the blessings of the New Testament.

11.8.0.en: Christ shows here the importance of spiritual striving for obtaining the Kingdom of Heaven: in proportion to the grace of the New Testament which John the Baptist prepared, spiritual striving is required to hold fast to it. Indeed the necessity of using force appears, that is, that a person compels himself and does not pamper his body, in order to leave his sins and hold fast to his prayers and his relationship with God, and also to seize every spiritual opportunity to draw near to God and enjoy fellowship with Him.

11.9.0.en: "Until John": because he is the last of the prophets of the Old Testament.

11.9.1.en: "If ye will receive it": if you had faith you would receive what I am about to say now.

11.9.2.en: If the aim of all the prophets was to prepare for the coming of Christ, then John is the forerunner who prepared the way for Him directly, and he came in the spirit of Elijah, so this is the fulfillment of the promise of the coming of Elijah, but in a spiritual way and not a bodily one, as will happen at the end of days (Mal 4:5-6), when Elijah comes in his body as he ascended in his body to heaven, to proclaim the voice of God before the last day of judgment.

11.9.3.en: And because of the importance of these teachings, Christ says: He who has inner ears in the heart to hear and believe, let him hear, because many of them were doubting, and did not believe that John is the one coming in the spirit of Elijah to prepare the way of the awaited Messiah, for if they believed this, it would mean their believing that He is the awaited Messiah; so He calls them to intense listening, understanding and faith.

11.9.4.en: In order to be strong in proclaiming the truth and holding fast to the commandments of God, you need detachment like John the Baptist. So do not pamper yourself with many lusts and ease for the body, and you will have a strong will in your spiritual striving and your worship, and then in your service and your proclaiming the name of Christ.

11.10.0.en: "This generation": He means the scribes and Pharisees and chief priests who refused to believe in Christ. "Children": that is, weak in their understanding and grasp of spiritual meanings and the word of God, and fickle in their opinions. "The markets": the place where the children gather to play.

11.10.1.en: Christ likens the leaders of the Jews, the scribes and Pharisees and others, who refused to believe in the call of John the Baptist, and likewise to believe in Christ, to a group of children playing in the markets of the villages and divided into two groups; one group of them plays the pipe and makes joyful, amusing movements, and the other group was not affected and delighted; then they began to mourn and show signs of grief, and the second group was not affected so as to mourn and beat the breast; that is, they failed to change their expressions.

11.10.2.en: What is meant by this likeness is that John the Baptist's call to repentance came with rebuke and grief over sin, and they refused to respond to him. Then Christ came proclaiming love and healing the sick to rejoice hearts, and they refused also.

11.11.0.en: "Neither eating nor drinking": that is, ascetic and detached, content with the least food.

11.11.1.en: "He hath a devil": because of his conduct, withdrawn from people in the wilderness, they supposed that, with his strange life, he dealt with demons.

11.11.2.en: "A gluttonous man, and a winebibber": an exaggeration by the elders of the Jews in accusing Christ, although He eats and drinks like the rest of people.

11.11.3.en: John the Baptist was an ascetic living in the wilderness, and instead of learning asceticism from him, they accused him of having a devil. But Jesus Christ lived among people eating and drinking like them, to make it easy for them to fulfill the commandments in ordinary life, and they accused Him of being absorbed in eating much and drinking wine, and this of course is not true, and they accused Him also of being a friend of tax collectors and sinners, because like them He loves gatherings of eating and drinking; whereas Christ sat with sinners to draw them to repentance, as He drew Matthew and Zacchaeus the tax collectors.

11.11.4.en: The leaders of the Jews are like children, that is, spiritually immature. But the disciples of Christ and His followers are the spiritually mature.

11.11.5.en: The children of Wisdom: those who believed in the call of John and the good news of Christ, for the righteousness of Wisdom appeared in her followers, that is, the followers of John the Baptist, and then of Christ, the Eternal Wisdom, and they believed His word; that is, the power of Wisdom and her righteousness appear in those who believe in her, and they are the disciples and the believers.

11.11.6.en: Do not be hasty in judging others lest you err, and do not be biased lest people's virtues turn into sins in your sight, but on the contrary, look for God in the virtues of others, to learn and be discipled at their hands, so that you love all, and grow in your life with God.

11.12.s.en: (4) The punishment of those who reject faith

11.12.0.en: After He had explained the faith to His hearers, and called them also by miracles, He rebuked them for the hardness of their hearts in refusing the faith, especially the cities in the region of Galilee, because He had performed many miracles in them. So He declared that the fate of Chorazin (a city in Galilee near Bethsaida and Capernaum) and Bethsaida (a city on the Sea of Tiberias) would be dreadful in eternal torment, because the clear teachings and miracles, which easily call people to faith, if they had been done in the ancient cities of Tyre and Sidon which were on the Mediterranean Sea (in present-day Lebanon), they would have repented long ago, using the signs of humbling oneself, such as wearing rough clothes like sackcloth, and putting ashes on the head.

11.12.1.en: And by this He shows how hard the hearts of the inhabitants of Chorazin and Bethsaida were, in refusing to believe in Christ.

11.13.0.en: On the last day of judgment, the punishment of Tyre and Sidon will be lighter than that of Chorazin and Bethsaida, because the latter two refused a great faith offered to them by Christ Himself.

11.13.1.en: And the meaning of this verse is that there are degrees in eternal torment, and that those who reject the good news of Christ and life with Him will have a punishment more severe than those who did not know Christ and lived in sin, such as the pagans. A person will be held accountable according to the divine graces that were declared to him, therefore you must live and apply what you have heard in your home and your church, so that these teachings may support you on the way of salvation, and not judge you on the day of judgment.

11.14.0.en: Christ speaks about Capernaum, which became the center of His preaching in Galilee, and He performed many miracles in it, which should have saved it so that it would find a place in heaven, but sadly its people became proud, and felt they were better than those around them, as if they were in heaven and the other cities lower than they, on the earth, and they refused to believe in Him; so the fate of this city is to descend to hell.

11.14.1.en: And the measure of the work of God's grace in Capernaum, had it been done in Sodom long ago, it would have repented and the divine judgment of burning would not have been carried out on it.

11.15.0.en: Then He affirms that the torment of Sodom on the day of judgment will be lighter than the torment of Capernaum, which rejected Him; both will perish, but the severity of the torment increases for Capernaum because of its rejection of Christ; and likewise everyone who today rejects the faith and the Christian way of life will have a greater punishment.

11.16.0.en: "At that time": that is, after His words about the pride of the cities to which He had preached and which rejected Him, and a severe punishment awaits them.

11.16.1.en: "Answered": it appears that some had put a question to Him about the fate of the students of the Law found in these cities, so He answered with a prayer:

11.16.2.en: "I thank thee": as a man, He offers thanks to God for His wisdom and His ordering of things.

11.16.3.en: "The wise and prudent": the scribes and Pharisees, wise in their own eyes, and proud of their knowledge. "Babes": the disciples, weak in their knowledge, but humble and obedient to His word.

11.16.4.en: "Even so": a confirmation of the preceding answer, that the grace of God is granted to the humble.

11.16.5.en: "Good pleasure": God's joy in granting His grace to the humble.

11.16.6.en: In this great conversation between the Son and the Father, Christ confesses and declares an important truth, which is that the knowledge of God is granted to the simple and humble, and those who are wise in their own eyes, that is, the proud, are deprived of it, for God does not give His glory to another.

11.17.0.en: "All things are delivered unto me of my Father": that is, the Son received the complete authority for the redemption and salvation of mankind, and the meaning of "delivered" is not that He did not have authority and then received it when He became incarnate, but it is a declaration to us as human beings that the Son has all the authority of the Father; for the Jews know God in the Old Testament, and so Christ, who appeared in the New Testament, makes known to them by Himself that He is God, who has all authority, because He is one with the Father in essence.

11.17.1.en: "No man knoweth the Son": that is, all human beings, however great their faith, will not know the whole essence of God, because they are limited and their knowledge is limited, so only God the Father is able to know the Son, because He is equal to Him in essence. "Neither knoweth any man the Father": just as all the human beings who believed in God in the Old Testament cannot know God the Father with perfect knowledge, so the only One who knows the Father is the Son, who has the same essence as the Father.

11.17.2.en: "He to whomsoever the Son will reveal him": these are the saints whom Christ makes to know more about God by His Holy Spirit, not everything, but more than other human beings, and that is because of their humility and their longing for the love of God. No one knows God except His own essence, because He is higher than human comprehension. So the Son knows the Father and the Father knows the Son, that is, God alone is the One who knows Himself. But God in His love revealed Himself to us through the Incarnation of the Son, who makes us know God in proportion to our humility, and these humble ones are the chosen, who enjoy the knowledge of God.

11.18.0.en: "Come unto me": a call to all human beings who feel their troubles and their need for salvation. But those immersed in the world and content with its lusts do not feel their need for Christ. "All ye that labour and are heavy laden": with the burden of sin, the reproach of conscience, the problems resulting from their sins, and all the pressures of life and its fears.

11.18.1.en: "I will give you rest": He did not promise human beings the prevention of afflictions, but promises them rest during them, since He bears them with them and for them, so they do not feel their weight, and are comforted and rejoice in fellowship with Him.

11.18.2.en: Christ became incarnate to bear our toils and our sins on the Cross, so His arms are open to lift from us our sins and all that results from them, so that we find our peace in Him, and He is able to order all the affairs of our life.

11.19.0.en: "My yoke": the yoke is the piece of wood placed on the necks of the animals that pull agricultural implements such as the plow, so bearing the yoke means bowing the neck, that is, humility, and enduring pain for the sake of Christ, and these are the marks of the followers of Christ.

11.19.1.en: "Learn of me": Christ is an example for us in all His conduct on earth, and He is the highest ideal for mankind. "Meek": He keeps His peace and inner calm, and is not stirred by any gain or loss.

11.19.2.en: "Lowly": He puts Himself beneath all, giving up all His glory.

11.19.3.en: "Rest unto your souls": meekness and lowliness are the way to obtaining salvation.

11.19.4.en: The Lord reassures us that His yoke is easy and light, because He bears it with us, and if two carry one load, the weight falls on the stronger. So if God, the stronger without limit, carries with us, He carries everything for us, so we feel no weariness at all, but enjoy fellowship with Him all along the way of our life, and behold His work in us and in the souls we deal with and serve.

11.19.5.en: Humble yourself under the feet of all, and you will know God and enjoy fellowship with Him...

11.19.6.en: Accept pain for God's sake, and you will see Him beside you encouraging you, and gladdening your heart, and lifting from you every pain and suffering, because He supports you in everything.

11.19.7.en: The purifying of the heart produces mercy and defeats the demons
